full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I disagree with the first pass's "KNOWN-VARIANT". Nothing in the reported numbers points to behaviour the literature doesn't already cover.

**1. This exact rule is a well-known, named rule.** Three colours, Moore neighbourhood, range 1, threshold 3 is "313" (R1/T3/C3/NM) in Mirek Wójtowicz's MCell catalogue. It is credited to David Griffeath and described as "the only three-color rule in the range-1 CCA rulespace that exhibits significant self-organization." It sports a number of distinct spiral types. So the textbook behaviour for this rule is spiral waves, not coarsening.

**2. The first pass picked the wrong reference phase.** The metastable "turbulent" phase it cited comes from Shalizi et al., whose figures use 4 colours. In that setting, at T=3 one finds "turbulence," which is metastable: spiral waves can form and take over the whole grid, but on finite lattices this doesn't always happen, and the turbulent phase can last a very long time. That describes the 4-colour rule (R1/T3/C4), not this 3-colour one. The overall phase picture still applies, though: at high thresholds you get static solid blocks (fixation); at intermediate thresholds, wave fronts form, travel for a while, then break up.

**3. Making the update random (p = 0.1) isn't a new twist either.** The founding paper on these automata already says that, started from random states, they typically nucleate locally periodic 'ram's horns' or spirals, and that the corresponding random processes produce 'forest fire' equilibria with large-scale stochastic wave fronts. Random versions were in the programme from the start. Bramson and Griffeath's cyclic particle systems are the continuous-time random counterpart: continuous-time Markov processes with stochastic rather than deterministic evolution. Rock-paper-scissors lattice models also cover the domain behaviour. In 1D, domains grow algebraically over time, while in 2D domains can break up, allowing long-term coexistence. That fits what you saw: all 3 types survive (entropy ≈ 1.0) and there are about 4 domains rather than one winner.

**4. Why the fingerprint doesn't look like textbook coarsening.** Correlation length ≈ 4.7 on a 64×64 grid, Moran's I ≈ 0.77, and about half of all changes being cyclic steps add up to noisy, patchy wave fronts that keep cycling. That is the stochastic-wave-front regime above, not coarsening that settles down. Passing the coarsening test is most likely a labelling side effect: it is a 3-colour rule that makes local patches. The same class also contains noisy-majority rules (p = 0.001), which really do coarsen. So the class merges two different known mechanisms that just look alike on these summary statistics.

**Genuine or artifact?** The pattern itself is real and well documented (excitable-media self-organisation). The "domain coarsening" label is the shaky part. One limit: I didn't find a paper giving this exact asynchronous T=3, 3-colour parameter set, but by your own criterion that's a rule-tuple gap, not a new behaviour. I also didn't read the 1991 papers in full.
